articles.title: Evolving climate architecture
articles.content: PAKISTAN stands at a crossroads as it prepares to attend COP31 in Turkiye next week. Every October, the Emissions Gap Report brings bad news, and every October we read it as a scorecard of how far the world is from Paris. This year, it is not a progress report. It is notice that the Paris benchmark has been breached. The United Nations Environment Programme’s 2026 report concludes that the chance to hold warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius with no or limited overshoot “is gone”. The task now is to “minimise overshoot and return to 1.5°C”. The target survives; its meaning has flipped. No longer a ceiling, 1.5°C is a line we will cross and then try to get back under. Even the “lowest possible” overshoot peaks at 1.7 to 1.8°C. For Pakistan, this is not abstract arithmetic. The gap between 1.5 and 1.8 is more poverty andheat in Jacobabad, wildermonsoons in Sindh, transboundaryfloods in Punjab, and fasterglacial meltin the upper Indus. The question is simple: who pays for the overshoot years? Just as the science matters most, the body that certifies it is going broke. For the first time in its history, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) “might not have the funds to finish an assessment report”,Naturewarned recently. Contributions have fallen since 2023, and Washington has walked away. The panel needs more than CHF 20 million ($24m) to survive until 2029, less than many single-donor projects in Islamabad. Nor can it agree on a timetable. In Addis Ababa last month, governments failed for the sixth meeting running to decide when its next reports come out. A small bloc wants the reports on emission cuts and adaptation delayed until after the 2028 global stocktake, the five-yearly review of progress under Paris. The reasons are procedural; the effect is political. For the most vulnerable countries, that delay is betrayal. Yet Pakistan, the self-declared ground zero of climate impacts, stayed away from the forum that certifies the evidence. We need some $47bn a year to 2030 but receive under $2bn. It is not for want of evidence. In August, the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) publishedHow the Climate of Pakistan Has Changed, a 45-year record and the most granular we have. Nights are warming faster than days, and springs across much of the country are up to 2.5°C warmer than in the 1980s and 1990s. Rain has become not scarcer but less dependable: the 2022 monsoon dumped up to 450 per cent above-average rain on the south, and three years later, the winter of 2024-25 brought a 67pc national deficit. That is the overshoot world in miniature. The EU’sParis Agreement Overshooting: Reversibility, Climate Impacts and Adaptation Needs(PROVIDE project), which studied exactly such risks, had an Islamabad partner, so the research clearly exists. What is missing is the habit of carrying it into the rooms where global science, and therefore, global money, is decided. The empty chair reflects a deeper reflex. Pakistan’s climate diplomacy still treats finance as something to ask for: grants, owed as a moral debt by those who caused the problem. The argument is right on the merits and increasingly beside the point. The COP29 goal of $300 billion a year is being hollowed out by the governments that pledged it, and what grant money remains goes to countries ready to absorb it. On that test, Pakistan fails. We need some $47bn a year to 2030 but receive under $2bn. The gap is not one of vulnerability but readiness. Meanwhile, a new architecture is taking shape elsewhere, and in one corner of it Pakistan already leads. At the World Bank-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok last month, Islamabad took the chair of the Borrowers’ Platform, which gives debtors what creditors have in the Paris Club: a place to pool data, compare terms, and bargain as a bloc. On Nov 1, it also assumed the chair of the G-24, the developing-country caucus at the IMF and World Bank. For a year then, Pakistan speaks for the debtors just as debt has become the main channel of climate finance. Disasters are paid for with borrowing, and each recovery loan makes the next shock harder to absorb. Pakistan, where debt servicing eats 43pc of the federal budget, is itself a textbook case. Of the $10bn pledged at Geneva after the 2022 floods, about $8.7bn came from lenders. We were asked to borrow our way out of a disaster we did little to cause. New instruments attack this chain link by link. Debt-pause clauses suspend repayments after a disaster; Grenada used one after Hurricane Beryl to defer about $30m. The V20, a bloc of finance ministers from the most climate-vulnerable countries, is building a Lifeline Fund that would pool members’ reserves into a $500m emergency facility. Africa’s new rating agency challenges unfair risk premiums; Mia Mottley’s Bridgetown Initiative demands cheaper, longer loans. Each treats climate as a balance sheet problem, and that is where the post-Paris order is taking shape. Pakistan now heads the borrowers’ table and leaves an empty chair at the scientists’ table. The two are linked: a debtor bloc that wants climate risk priced into debt terms needs credible, nationally owned evidence, and the IPCC is where such evidence gains global standing. Four steps follow before Antalya. First, rejoin the science table: pay into the IPCC trust fund, attend the resumed session in December, and back the least developed countries and small islands on a 2028 timeline. Second, put the PMD record to work in AR7, the next Nationally Determined Contributions, and the annual budgets. Third, trade appeals for readiness, with bankable adaptation projects, accredited national entities and climate tagging in the budget. Fourth, use the Borrowers’ Platform chair to make debt-pause clauses standard in sovereign lending and to tie debt and climate together at the stocktake. The world has moved past the Paris target and is moving past COP as the only place where climate is decided. The winds of change are blowing elsewhere. Pakistan should stop treating COPs as tourist destinations and start engaging where the rules are written.
articles.author: Ali Tauqeer Sheikh

articles.title: Turning of the American tide
articles.content: THE election results in America this week portend a sea change, and they have important ramifications for Pakistan. The Democrats havetakenboth the House and the Senate in a rout that reached Texas and Kansas. Anger over living costs, tariffs, and thewar on Iranall played their part. For the remaining two years of his term, President Donald Trump will face a Congress armed with subpoena power and eager to use it. This is no distant affair for us. Much of the world has spent two years trying to cope with Trump. Meanwhile, the leadership in Pakistan flamboyantly embraced him, though let’s not underestimate how well that worked. It got us lower tariffs, a White House lunch, and, above all, a central role when the Iran war needed an exit ramp. The question now is what that embrace will cost us as the man on the receiving end of it begins to lose his grip on Washington. Pakistan has veered too close to Trump, and this might not go down well in the near future. The April ceasefire that we helped broker was a genuine achievement, and I said so at the time. The memorandum that followed in June has since collapsed, but the credit earned in those weeks still stands. Yet all of it could well come to be overshadowed by the single act of having nominated Trump for a Nobel Peace Prize in so conspicuous and overly generous a manner. Showering the man with extravagant praise in highly public settings might have worked to win him over in the short term. But the praise kept coming long after the point had been made. In September, he was telling the UN General Assembly that our prime ministercreditshim with saving 30 million lives. Last month, on the day the Nobel went to someone else, the prime minister was on X lauding his “historic role” in South Asia. These things do not expire. There is a risk they get tagged onto Pakistan in the years to come, once Americans settle on their verdict of this presidency. What looks clever in one season reads very differently at a hearing in the next. Even more dangerous is the fact that the Trump family’s business dealings might come under congressional investigation.Reutersreported in September that probes could begin as early as February, with Trump-linked crypto firms of particular interest. Senator Richard Blumenthal, who is in line to chair an investigations panel, has promised to use his subpoena power. The same senator was asking questions about World Liberty Financial’s Pakistan deal in May last year. If any ties lead back here, they could tie the country to the affair; the threads are already in public view. In January, our finance minister signed a memorandum with a World Liberty affiliate concerning its USD1 stablecoin. In September, the defence ministry placed a limited order with Powerus, a drone company in which two of Trump’s sons are investors. No wrongdoing has been established. The White House denies any conflict of interest, and as of July the stablecoin deal had produced no known transactions at all. But I have described that memorandum as an instrument of access, and access is exactly what investigators will want to look into. What looks clever in one season reads very differently at a hearing in the next. These risks, however, are rooted more in optics and perceptions than in realpolitik. Pakistan’s thrust to find a place in the new regional order emerging in the Middle East must continue unabated. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, and the Tehran huddle I wrote about last week, which Field Marshal Asim Munir himself proposed, have a logic of their own that does not depend on who chairs which committee in Washington. Whatever the fallout for Pakistan, the changing of the political tide in America will be an American affair first and foremost. The most likely outcome is that the Trump administration comes to be consumed by its wrangling with the new Congress and loses its moorings in foreign policy. A White House fighting hearings and subpoenas at home will have little bandwidth for the world. This could produce a hazardous moment. A beleaguered and irrational president might try an adventure abroad to distract from his troubles at home, and the adventure is ready to hand. The blockade of Iran remains in place, reports in September said he saw a fresh bombing campaign as likely after the midterms, and Iran’s Supreme Leader warned on Wednesday that the war’s scope will widen if the attacks are repeated. But that seems unlikely given the stakes. This is the war voters have just punished him for, and on the eve of the vote he himself cast doubt on resuming strikes. What is more likely is an acceleration in the pace with which America withdraws from its commitments to underwrite global order, particularly its military posture in the Middle East. I argued in April that the price of getting out of this war would be a disorderly exit from the region altogether. A Congress that owes its majority partly to anger over this war will be in no hurry to fund the next one. The Gulf monarchies have seen their American protector fail to shield them from Iranian missiles, and they are drawing their own conclusions. All this will spur the search for a new security architecture among the powers of the region, a search that will definitely include Pakistan. Three times in our history, in the 1960s, the 1980s and the 2000s, an American embrace brought dollars and a growth spurt, and each time the money stopped when Washington’s interest moved on. This time it has brought more photographs than dollars. Ironically enough, this turning inward of the United States might just be the push Pakistan needs to learn to stand on its own feet. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: Decreasing faith
articles.content: CHRISTIANITY is treading a slow, painful path to its own Calvary. Two thousand years after its emergence as an alternative to Judaism, it is succumbing to a 21st-century malaise — the disparity between the ultra-rich and the irredeemable poor. It has been reported that a community of Benedictine nuns in Poland needs $1 million urgently to preserve their 800-year-old abbey, which is almost half as old as Christianity itself. Until now, the abbey has been supported by the European Union and sustained by the sale of its own tomatoes and preserves, supplemented by income derived from visitors. (A contemplative order in Karachi — the Monastery of the Angels in Malir — similarly relies upon income from its bakery and confectionery). One would have imagined that Catholic-rich countries like Brazil and Mexico, or the Vatican (worth $5 billion) and the Vatican Bank ($5.4bn) would help subvent the Polish monastery. Apparently, Peter and his pence are not so easily parted. The predicament within the Catholic church is not unique. Almost 500 years ago, the English King Henry VIII disbanded “over 800 Catholic monasteries, abbeys, priories, and nunneries” across his kingdom. They owned roughly “a quarter of all cultivated land in England and held vast amounts of gold, silver, and jewels”. King Henry diverted their wealth to his private coffers and demanded their loyalty to himself as the head of his new Church of England. The Catholic church’s predicament is not unique. Today, that Church of England is as indigent as its progenitor King Henry once was. More than 8,000 churches across the UK have closed “due to declining congregations or structural issues”. They have been converted into “private homes, shops, or community spaces” — into anything but a mosque. Out of roughly 16,000 Church of England buildings, only one (St Mark’s in Peckham, SE London) eventually became a mosque, but only after it had already been used as a scrap yard and a factory. Deconsecrated churches and parish properties in the UK are listed on ‘LoopNet UK Churches for Sale’ or The Church of Scotland Properties for Sale. That decline has spread across the channel to France where ‘deconsecrated chapels, abbeys, and former convents’ are put on the market. Even in Italy, ‘Immobiliare Italiano Church Properties/ Monasteries’ offer online deconsecrated churches, chapels, monasteries, and abbeys. Prices range from a minimum of €30,000–€85,000 to many millions for larger buildings. Interestingly, for the first time in its history, the Church of England today has a female Archbishop of Canterbury. By tradition, since the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, British monarchs (including queens) have been Supreme Governors of the Church of England. The United Kingdom will not readily admit it, but it is technically at par with other theocracies: Afghanistan, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, and the Vatican. Another ‘first’ occurred when last year, out of the 91 nationalities represented in the Roman Catholic College of Cardinals, 116 of the cardinal electors voted in an American — Robert F. Prevost, originally from Chicago’s South side — to the papacy. He chose the title Pope Leo XIV deliberately. The name echoes the proactive history of earlier Leos — Leo I, who persuaded Attila the Hun to spare Rome; Leo X, who excommunicated Martin Luther, causing the Protestant Reformation; and the modernist Leo XIII, whose encyclical Rerum Novarum (1891) addressed issues such as “industrial labour, workers’ rights, and Catholic social teaching”. Reports of Pope Leo XIV’s health are a cause of concern. But he will survive his secular counterparts — his fellow American President Donald Trump and the neo-American Benjamin Netanyahu, both of whom are struggling to remain electorally relevant. Voters in Pakistan are also suffering from a diminution of faith in democracy. They have watched political parties join fists against popularity. And now those erstwhile allies stand pitted against each other. As one 17th-century Royalist said, after being defeated by the parliamentarian Roundheads: “Now that you have done with us, go fight amongst yourselves.” Of late, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman has fallen out with the present hybrid form of governance. Over the years, he used his narrow electoral base to negotiate admittance into the corridors of power but it was never large enough to make him more than a petulant spoiler. Like Trump and Netanyahu, he craves relevance. Who was it who said: ‘Power reveals who we are, not who we pretend to be’? Prof J.H. Plumb (a specialist in British 18th-century history) defined history as “a dream made of actual events”. Had he been alive, he would have written about our political shenanigans as a recurring nightmare, “made up of actual events”.
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: AI & climate adaptation
articles.content: THIS month in Antalya, artificial intelligence will have its own day at the 31st Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The Antalya Pledge on AI asks countries to align the rapid growth of AI with global climate goals by addressing AI’s skyrocketing energy demand. The pledge requires AI companies to disclose their data centres’ energy use and shift to clean energy. The COP31 presidency has described the draft pledge as a “political” commitment on how AI is “designed, procured, powered, deployed, measured and managed” in support of climate action. However, the discussion so far has centred largely on how AI is powered rather than on how it can be leveraged to help vulnerable countries adapt to a warming world. From extreme weather that left 87.5 million people facing acute food insecurity last year to drought draining Middle Eastern reservoirs and deadly heat in South Asia, climate change is impacting harvests, water availability, health, and livelihoods globally. AI can help communities, governments, farmers, and humanitarian organisations anticipate climate-related risks, protect essential resources, and respond faster to disasters. It can proactively convert climate data into actionable decisions that can save lives and reduce losses from adverse climate events. AI is already proving valuable for climate adaptation. In India’s Andhra Pradesh, a pilot that sent groundnut farmers AI-based advice on the best time to sow by text message in the local language raised average yields by 30 per cent. In Bihar, communities that received AI-based flood alerts faced 30pc lower medical costs after flooding due to earlier evacuations and timely preventative health measures. In Chile, forest sensors analysed by AI detect wildfires about 12 minutes faster than traditional watchtowers. In each case, AI turned data into timely information that people could act on. Pakistan has also taken steps in this direction. Since October 2025, the Met Office has used MAZU, a Chinese AI-based weather and early-warning system, to improve its forecasts of extreme weather. However, its nine-kilometre resolution is too coarse to capture highly localised weather such as flash floods, and Pakistan’s limited radar network restricts the local data it needs. Without such data and adequate response capacity, AI tools can produce unreliable forecasts. AI can convert climate data into actionable decisions. The Antalya Pledge gives Pakistan an opportunity to ensure that adaptation becomes part of the global conversation on AI and climate. To connect the AI pledge to climate adaptation, Pakistan can propose an adaptation-focused lens, with specific language on open climate data, locally adaptable AI models, and shared computing capacity — the building blocks that vulnerable countries like Pakistan need to use AI effectively. Such proposals will carry more weight if they come from many voices rather than just one. Working through platforms such as the Climate Vulnerable Forum can allow Pakistan to build a joint position with other climate-vulnerable countries and bring their shared priorities to the climate summit’s AI day. For these commitments to be measured, reported, and funded they must be anchored in the wider climate process. Calling for the integration of AI into the Global Goal on Adaptation will ensure that AI-enabled tools are recognised in the indicators adopted at COP30 to track progress and are eligible for the tripled adaptation finance called for by 2035. At home, Pakistan’s multipronged strategy to combat climate change can include: aligning its AI policy’s sector roadmaps with the priorities of its National Adaptation Plan, strengthening its weather monitoring network, improving climate data-sharing across federal and provincial institutions, and training forecasters, researchers and officials to use these tools. At present, the global scale of planned investment in AI contrasts sharply with the persistent shortfall in climate adaptation finance. Only 32 countries host AI data centres, and Microsoft, Google, Meta and Amazon together plan to spend about $725 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026. For these countries, the pledge’s focus on clean energy matters. But for developing countries, which received just $26bn of more than the $310bn a year needed by 2035 to adapt to climate change, AI’s value as a tool for adaptation matters just as much. Pakistan comes to Antalya with a clean energy transition shaped by its own citizens, acknowledgement of the need to accelerate clean energy, and an experience of what climate change costs. A pledge that makes AI’s power supply cleaner is a welcome step. One that also puts AI to work helping vulnerable countries adapt to climate change would make it far more meaningful. Maha Qasim is a climate & sustainability expert. Tahreem Fatima is a sustainability professional.
articles.author: Maha Qasim | Tahreem Fatima

articles.title: Blue wave
articles.content: THE politics of toxicity and confrontation at home and abroad have led to a severe setback for American President Donald Trump. His Republican Party experienced adrubbingat Tuesday’s midterm polls, with the Democrats riding a decisive blue wave to power in both houses of the US Congress, and taking control of the American government’s legislative arm. The Democrats managed wins in deeply red states, indicating the widespread dissatisfaction with Mr Trump’s style of governance. For most Americans, the unpopularwar of choice with Iranand the cost-of-living crisis it has led to were reason enough to punish the Republicans at the ballot box. Mr Trump, referring to the electoral pummelling, admitted that “part of it was Iran”. While domestically the economy and the Trump administration’s abrasive immigration policies are likely to dominate the agenda, the rest of the world would like to know if America will change course on the foreign front. In his second term, Mr Trump has turned the old international order upside down, pushed around old allies, downplayed climate change, and talked of taking over other states’ territory. His biggest foreign folly — in partnership with Israel — has been the war against Iran. Perhaps feeling the heat, just before the midterms, Mr Trump had announced he was ending a multibillion-dollar aid programme to Israel. It is unlikely the decision was a moral one emanating from genuine displeasure with the Zionist state’s murderous policies. More likely, it was a last-ditch attempt to court MAGA voters, many of whom increasingly question the subservience of the American political class to Israel at the expense of their own country. In fact, expectations of a radical shift on the foreign policy front may be premature. For one, Democratic presidents, too, have launched foreign wars, and many among the supposedly ‘liberal’ party are staunch votaries of Israel. Moreover, while the Democrats will enjoy greater legislative oversight, partially limiting Mr Trump’s ability to wage and fund foreign wars, the president retains veto powers that can override Congress. This means that those Democrats — and Republicans — opposed to American military action abroad must make a serious effort to halt strikes on Iran and prevent taxpayers’ dollars from funding Israel’s genocidal campaigns against the Palestinians. While Mr Trump does not usually learn from his errors, perhaps seeing the response of the American voters he may attempt a wiser course. Candidate Trump had promised no more ‘forever wars’; President Trump must now extricate himself from a needless war he launched against Iran. It is time he heeded the call of the voters and worked on rebuilding and uniting his country, instead of destroying others.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: New LPG policy
articles.content: EACH winter, millions of working-class households across the country face the same ordeal. LPG, long considered the poor man’s fuel, is now what many middle-class families use for cooking and heating. An increasing number of homes lacking piped connections in cities end up buying cylinders as temperatures fall. Gas rationing due to shortages caused by dwindling domestic gas reserves, together with increasing tariffs on imported RLNG, is boosting the demand for LPG. Whenwintersets in, demand jumps, supply tightens, and traders hoard stocks. This year, as the petroleum minister told the National Assembly last month, the closure of the western borders has disrupted import shipments, which account for 70pc of LPG imports, exacerbating the shortages. The Saudi Aramco price, to which local LPG is linked, has alsorisento $705 per tonne and the fuel is selling at Rs700-800 per kilogram — well above the official ceiling. For families already stretched by inflation, even LPG has become something to ration. It is against this backdrop that the government hasannounceda new LPG policy that directs four SOEs to resume bulk imports through government-to-government and business-to-business deals. Their base prices will be published, giving the market a landed-cost benchmark. The policy also scraps the discretionary quota system. Locally produced gas will be sold through open auctions, which should cut out the intermediaries who profit from the existing arrangement. The gap between auction proceeds and the SOEs’ import parity price will go into a dedicated fund, allowing the government to sell LPG at Rs300-350 per kilogram to BISP beneficiaries, without burdening the government budget or widening the fiscal deficit. Enforcementis the weak point. It always has been. The authorities have issued many price and market rules that were never properly implemented. The Competition Commission of Pakistan, the National Explosives and Petroleum Safety Agency, and district administrations are all expected to act against collusion. They will have to be present at the retail level, where distributors have long kept the margins meant for consumers. The auctions need watching too, since a handful of large bidders could capture them. If the policy is enforced effectively, it could potentially help end shortages and slash prices. But the question remains whether it will.
articles.author: Editorial
